text:
Winamp actually does not use a single engine for everything. It has its own set of native visualizations, but it's become a bit of a hotbed for community contributions. They introduced an SDK, and it's just sort of an open field, where anybody can create their own plugin for the visualizations. There are tons of them. So, there's the old Winamp visualization plugins, there's the so-called 2D, and then there's the 3D.

3D being the most interesting and the most popular, and then there's the 4D, which is really just a spin on 3D. So, how does it work? Basically, it's all driven by the spectrum of frequencies of what's playing. So, you know, Winamp grabs the audio, runs it through a fast Fourier transform to get the frequencies, and that's just a data stream. It's a set of values, it's got numbers, it's got a number for each frequency, a number for how loud that frequency is. And then, the plugin can use that data to generate the visual.

So, the 3D, for instance, the 3D plugin will generate a grid, and then it will have a 3D grid of points, and then it will take the frequency values and turn them into the height of the grid, so the louder the frequency, the higher the point. And then, it'll just render that. But you can do whatever you want. The SDK, the visual plugin SDK, is actually pretty simple. You can take a frequency and do whatever you want. So, you could make the color change, you could make the grid spin, you could make it move, you could do anything you want. So, people have made, you know, the classic 3D grid, they've made bubbles, they've made it look like a galaxy, they've made it look like a star, they've made it look like a blob, they've made it look like the solar system, they've made it look like a bunch of balls. There's tons of plugins out there, and they all do completely different things. But it's all just a data stream, it's just numbers. And the plugin is just interpreting those numbers and turning them into something that you can look at. And then, the way it does it, it's very fast. The Winamp 3D plugin, it's a direct3D plugin, so it uses the GPU, so it's pretty fast. And then, it'll update every frame, so it's like 30 or 60 frames a second. And it'll just take the data, it'll use it, and then it'll move things around, and it'll spin things around, and it'll do whatever it wants to do. And that's pretty much how it works. And then, the 2D stuff is much simpler, it's just a waveform. But, yeah, 3D is the most interesting.
